newsitem.title: USA: Clinton expects more Saudi cooperation on bombing.
newsitem.headline: Clinton expects more Saudi cooperation on bombing.

text.p: President Bill Clinton told Saudi Arabia's defence minister on Tuesday the United States expects better cooperation in the investigation into a truck bomb attack last year against Americans in the Saudi kingdom.
"We've received some cooperation with respect to the investigation and the president made clear today that we expect to receive more," White House spokesman Mike McCurry said.

The visit by Saudi Defence Minister Prince Sultan, heading a high-level ministerial delegation, was meant to reaffirm close U.S.-Saudi relations marred by U.S. concerns over the probe into the truck bombing last June 25 that killed 19 American servicemen near Dhahran.

The prince said after meeting Clinton that he hoped he allayed U.S. concerns about the investigation. "I think if you ask the American side you will find a positive response that they were left with," he told reporters.
McCurry said Clinton was "delighted" to have received reassurances from the prince.
Washington has complained publicly that Saudi Arabia is not sharing enough information on its investigation.

A White House statement said that during the talks, Clinton "stressed his determination to protect the security of American troops stationed in Saudi Arabia, and they discussed our cooperation in the fight against terrorism."

In a reminder of the continued threat in Saudi Arabia, the U.S. embassy there warned Americans in the kingdom on Tuesday to raise their guard against further attacks following fresh threats by a leading Islamic dissident.
Clinton reaffirmed the U.S. commitment to ensuring security and stability in the Gulf region and pledged to "work with Saudi Arabia to respond to any external threats to our mutual interests."

Prince Sultan said he and Clinton did not discuss Saudi Arabia's interest in purchasing perhaps as many as 100 F-16 fighters to replace their ageing fleet of 114 F-5s. Israel has expressed concern about a possible deal.
"This visit was not here to conclude armament deals or contracts," the prince said. He spoke in Arabic translated into English by Prince Bandar, the Saudi ambassador to America.
Generally speaking, both sides spoke glowingly of the state of U.S.-Saudi relations.
"I would like to reaffirm the especially strong relationship between the United States and Saudi Arabia," said Prince Sultan.
McCurry said: "U.S.-Saudi relations are strong and will remain so. Our countries have been friends in peace and allies in war."

Prince Sultan, representing his brother King Fahd, arrived on Monday at the head of a delegation that included foreign, oil and trade ministers and a deputy finance minister. They will stay until Friday.

Prince Sultan was to meet Defence Secretary William Cohen on Wednesday and Secretary of State Madeleine Albright on Thursday to discuss, among other topics, the Middle East peace process. The prince described Clinton's Middle East policy as "steady and consistent."
Following the White House gathering, Saudi oil minister Ali Naimi met with acting U.S. Energy Secretary Charles Curtis to discuss world oil markets and global warming policies.

"The most important thing to come out of this was general reconfirmation of how important Saudi Arabia is as an oil supplier to the United States and to the world," said U.S. Associate Deputy Energy Secretary Kyle Simpson.
"They expressed what we've known all along -- their desire to see a stable world market," he told reporters after a 2-1/2 hour meeting.
